searchText: Isn't this almost exactly how zkS[tn]arks work? ~~Aren't they for more general polynomial stuff?~~ You can do a ton more than just set membership with those, right? D thought the core of them was just "is x part of set y"? I'm certainly no expert, but I believe that is kind of the canonical and simplest use case. It is how Tornado works for example, "is this note in the set (without knowing the set of all notes)?" And anyone can add a note to the set without revealing the note being added. If you don't need secrecy in set generation there is maybe something simpler? No, definitely no secrecy. I'd just publish the whole set if it wasn't gigantic. Ah, Bob doesn't have A or B because of data availability, not secrecy. I misunderstood. Yeah, exactly. I didn't make that clear, I don't think it was possible for you to guess 😛 Do you need probabilistic guarantees or absolute guarantees? A bloom filter, for example, will give you kinda high guarantees if the filter is big enough relative to data size. Hm, yeah. I had come across the term "secure bloom filter" in my spelunking into academia That sounds like a synonym for "exceedingly large bloom filter". 🙂 It does, doesn't it? 😛 check out efficient sparse merkle trees, those might fit your requirements For merkle trees, you need more than *just* `C` though right? You would need `C` plus some random set of other things. <@689161464829050960> If you can solve this problem it would be a huge boon to air/merkle-drops. 🙂 Ha, if there isn't an already existing primitive, I'm certainly not going to be the one to find it. Yeah, that's the problem we had. If Alice doesn't reveal the entire set, you can't prove arbitrary members. afaik, not for sparse merkle trees; in a sparse merkle tree each leaf is an unique element and it's hash is the path to that element, more or less ``` This is due to an intractably large Merkle tree that reserves a unique leaf l for every conceivable key digest. The hash of a key k determines l, and k is a (non-)member if the attribute a ∈ l is set to a0 and a1, respectively. Hence, the resulting tree structure contains 2N leaves at all times, and (non-)membership can be proven by presenting an audit path for leaf H(k). ``` What is an audit path for leaf `H(k)`? I assumed, naively, that it would require other blobs from `S` the path is the binary representation of the hash function output; i.e. you have a balanced binary tree and based on the binary representation of `H(k)` you take a path down the tree here's a go implementation: https://github.com/pylls/gosmt (paper link is in the readme) 🤔 For sparse siblings you can *guess* empty and be right most of the time, how do you handle the case when it is non-empty? How many set elements would you need to even approach the possibility of that happening?
